newsitem.title: FRANCE: Critics want French bill scrapped, not amended.
newsitem.headline: Critics want French bill scrapped, not amended.

text.p: A senior Gaullist parliamentarian offered an amendment to a fiercely contested French immigration bill on Wednesday removing an obligation on citizens and mayors to report the movements of foreigners.

The amendment by Pierre Mazeaud, chairman of the National Assembly's legislation committee, was aimed at rescuing Prime Minister Alain Juppe's conservative government from a torrent of protests by artists, intellectuals and students.
But the opposition Socialist party, and the organisers of petitions calling for civil disobedience, immediately demanded that the bill be scrapped, not amended.
Socialist spokesman Francois Hollande said the legislation contained other "extremely dangerous" provisions. "That is why we Socialists demand the bill be purely and simply withdrawn."

Thousands of members of France's academic, professional and artistic elite had signed appeals condemning the bill, which would have required citizens to report to the police when a foreign guest left their home.
The bill is aimed at tightening up controls to prevent Third World citizens on short-term tourist visas from overstaying and working illegally in France.

Critics accuse the government of borrowing from the policies of the extreme-right National Front in a bid to win back voters. Some compared the measure to the obligation to denounce the presence of Jews during the Nazi occupation of France.
Civil rights groups, student unions and left-wing parties plan big demonstrations in Paris on Thursday, Saturday and next Tuesday, when the National Assembly is due to give the bill a second reading.
Mazeaud proposed that government prefects rather than mayors should be responsible for issuing "accommodation certificates" to foreigners subject to visa requirements.
The foreigner himself would have to hand in the form to an immigration official on leaving the country.
Mazeaud said the bill would otherwise have been struck down by the Constitutional Council, France's constitutional watchdog.

Interior Minister Jean-Louis Debre, denying a report in the weekly Le Canard Enchainee that he had threatened to resign if his bill was changed, said he was satisfied with the amendment which met the aim of fighting illegal immigration effectively.
The National Front ridiculed what it called the government's "capitulation to...the show-biz rich and the caviar left" and demanded a referendum on immigration.
After standing by the original bill in defiant statements at the weekend, Juppe indicated on Tuesday he was willing to climb down on the most controversial parts of the legislation.
He told parliament the government was "open to discussion" if lawmakers found alternative ways of checking that foreigners really did leave the country when their visas expired.

Francois Leotard, leader of the centre-right Union for French Democracy, junior partners in Juppe's coalition, said in a radio interview on Wednesday that he would not have reported to the police a foreign guest who left his home.
Referring to the protests by artists and intellectuals, Leotard told Europe-1 radio: "I think we have to listen to those people and not treat their action with arrogance."
